title: Rules Turned Into Requirements: Consumer, Payment, Invoicing and Platform Regulation
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/36-commerce-regulation/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Modalities, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for and the published chapter did not have (a roadmap, a conclusion paragraph that answers the opening, Part VIII's closing) and the invoicing mandates lost from the published page in a later edit (restored from the chapter's history); these are listed under decision_log.

know: The four questions that read a law as a requirement (who is in scope; what it requires in data terms; which system of record holds that and which channels show it; when it applies and how compliance is tested), and the method table that applies them to eight rules.

The rules as the chapter states them from their official texts, by what they touch: withdrawal and refund clocks and the order button (Consumer Rights Directive), the 30-day prior price (Omnibus), strong customer authentication, verification of payee and pending PSD3/PSR, e-invoicing (Germany 2025 to 2028; Belgium from 1 January 2026, whether it binds a Dutch supplier without a Belgian establishment not settled by the sources; ViDA from 1 July 2030; a planned Dutch mandate), the DSA and GPSR, the ESPR destruction ban and digital product passport, the PPWR, the European Accessibility Act, NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act, the AI Act and the Data Act; and the US contrast.
Kestrel & Pine's four rules through four doors, its March 2027 regulatory calendar (maintain, prepare and watch rows, each with an owner), the four ways to run compliance and the GPSR worked example.
believe: Most rules are data requirements with a date, not page requirements; each belongs in a system of record.
Dates slip while scope holds, transposition multiplies the calendar, and partners enforce before regulators do.
The platform absorbs some rules (the button, the banner, the card scope of its checkout, its own pages' accessibility), never the merchant's data rows.
can_do: Turn a rule into a requirement card: scope, data requirement, system of record, channels, test, date and owner.
Keep a regulatory calendar with an owner per row who owns the fact, read against the official source each quarter, and say which size or role threshold switches a row on.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture with no legal background; most of all the engineering or product lead who receives regulatory demands through customers, marketplaces and auditors and wants one door instead of four, and the finance or operations owner who will own calendar rows. Also useful to an architect deciding which hubs regulation justifies.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side; roughly what an API, a database and a report are.
Kestrel & Pine, its people (Noor Visser, Sanne de Wit, Milan Petrov, Teun Baas, Daniel Okafor), its 2026 and 2027 incidents in outline, Waypoint and the names of the sixteen failure patterns.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, 'system', 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, business models and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From Parts II and III: product, variant, SKU and GTIN with one owning system per attribute; prices selected once at order placement and frozen, dated copies compared daily; checkout creating the order once with payment pending; authorization, capture, settlement and payout; one order record with three status lines; tax from three facts, one invoice per shipment, credit notes as the only correction.

From the Part VIII introduction and chapters 34 and 35: a checkout that accepts a real purchase also accepts 48,000 attempts with stolen cards by the same behavior; each chapter adds a column to the ownership map; chapter 34's identities and keys with owners and the April 2027 security baseline; chapter 35's one person in many systems, the per-system role, request-action and retention map, consent with evidence on the customer master, the one-month request clock and the October 2027 request orchestrator.
does_not_know: Directive versus regulation, transposition, application date.

Right of withdrawal, prior price, GPSR and responsible person, DSA trader traceability, EAA and WCAG, SCA and verification of payee, e-invoice and Peppol, ViDA, PPWR and producer responsibility, ESPR and the digital product passport, NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act, AI Act Art. 50, Data Act switching.
Economic nexus, marketplace-facilitator laws, the INFORM Act.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a product-information rule enforced by a marketplace, the reader reads it as a requirement and places the work in a system of record, rather than fixing listings by hand.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand's marketplace connector starts rejecting listings because a product-safety regulation requires every online offer to show the manufacturer's name and address and safety warnings. The marketplace team proposes filling the gaps from a spreadsheet. Using only this chapter: how should the brand read this rule, and where should the work land?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Read it with the four questions. Scope: a trader offering products to EU consumers at a distance, so every product, own-brand and third-party. Data: the manufacturer's name and address, a responsible person in the EU where the manufacturer is outside it, identification including a picture, and warnings in a language the consumer understands: four attributes per product. System of record: the PIM, syndicated to every storefront and marketplace, not the connector or a spreadsheet, which are copies with no owner. Test: publication blocked when a field is missing. A calendar row with the date and an owner who owns the product facts. The marketplace enforced the rule before any regulator did, which is why partner notices need an owner too.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what the prior-price rule requires in data terms.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A shop plans a Black Friday banner 'was €199, now €149' for a jacket it sold at €179 in an autumn campaign that ended three weeks earlier, and its prices are copied into several systems. Using only this chapter: which 'was' price is lawful, and what must the shop have to show it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Under the Omnibus Directive the prior price is the lowest price the trader applied in at least the 30 days before the reduction, so the lawful 'was' price is €179, not €199. Showing it needs a 30-day price history per SKU per country, held as a legal record in the pricing system of record, with the strike-through computed from it and checked before every campaign; a shop whose prices live in several copies cannot produce that history.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say how a merchant should keep track of rules and what the way rules arrive teaches.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A Dutch apparel brand with about 300 employees sells online in three EU countries and to business customers in Belgium and Germany. In two years, rules reached it through a marketplace's rejections, an agency audit, a customer refusing PDF invoices and an auditor's newsletter. Using only this chapter: how should it keep track of rules from now on, and what do those arrivals teach?
acceptance_criteria.expected: One regulatory calendar with a row per applicable rule: date, official source, what it requires of the company, an owner who owns the fact (mostly finance, operations and merchandising rather than engineering) and a status (maintain, prepare, watch), read against the official source each quarter; once the company owns a PIM, an OMS or a price history, each row becomes a requirement card tied to the system-of-record map with its test in the release process. The arrivals show that rules are public years before they apply, that dates slip while scope holds, that a directive becomes national laws with their own dates, that partners such as marketplaces and business customers enforce first, and that scope follows size and role. On e-invoicing: the German mandate does not bind a Dutch issuer, the sources do not settle whether the Belgian one does, and business customers in both countries ask for the structured format anyway.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That a rule about showing an earlier price can require a price history the merchant has never stored, so engineering needs a data source, a collection process and a page change, and that learning of it just before it applies leaves little time (the Long Fuse); that rules also touch returns, product details, invoices and unsold goods; the four questions for each requirement (which data, who owns it, how it is tested, when it must work); that legal interpretation and national differences still need care; Eva's price, product information, checkout and return as the places rules apply. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's four rules through four doors and its 2027 regulatory calendar, and the dated official texts of EU and national rules.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: Which laws change what a commerce platform must do, by when, and how do you read them as requirements?
thesis.claim: The consumer, product-safety, invoicing and sustainability rules that reach an EU shop (withdrawal and refund clocks since 2014, the 30-day prior price since 2022, product-safety fields since December 2024, e-invoicing mandates from 2025 to 2030, the unsold-apparel destruction ban since July 2026) are data requirements: a field, a history, a dated event or a record that belongs in a system of record. Read each by scope, required data, owning system, a check that the data exists, and date, and keep one calendar whose row owners own that data.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that regulation is the legal department's concern, met by page changes (a banner, a label, a template) when a lawyer or a partner raises it, and that a hosted platform keeps its merchants compliant.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim keeps a calendar of the rules that apply to it, gives each row an owner who owns the fact, and puts the field, history or clock into the system that owns it before the date, instead of learning of a rule from whoever enforces it first. Four rules reached Kestrel & Pine through four doors it did not own: product-safety fields through marketplace listing rejections in December 2024 (three weeks of spreadsheet work); the European Accessibility Act through an agency audit in May 2025 (about 140 findings); structured invoicing through a Belgian business customer that stopped accepting PDFs in December 2025 (Peppol connected in six weeks; whether the Belgian mandate binds a Dutch supplier is not settled by the sources, but its Belgian customers' bookkeeping expects Peppol); and the ESPR ban on destroying unsold apparel through an auditor's newsletter in June 2026, weeks before it applied on 19 July 2026. In March 2027 Noor Visser and Sanne de Wit wrote the 2027 regulatory calendar with an owner per row, most of them not engineers; for the GPSR row, a PIM rule from Q3 2027 blocks publication without the four fields, after a clean-up of about 850 third-party variants.
thesis.how_why: The texts state their obligations as data: the prior price is the lowest price applied in at least the 30 days before a reduction, the refund is due within 14 days of the withdrawal notice, the GPSR lists the manufacturer, responsible person, identification and warnings each offer must show, and the ESPR asks for a yearly disclosure of discarded unsold products. Such a record exists only where one system owns the fact; a price in seven copies or a field kept in a connector cannot produce it. Rules are usually public two to four years before they apply, directives become national laws with their own dates, and marketplaces and business customers enforce them on dates of their own, so a merchant with no calendar meets each rule through whichever partner enforces it first. The hosted platform ships the order button, the cookie banner, the card scope of its checkout and the accessibility of its own pages, and leaves the merchant's price history, product fields, packaging and disposition records.

supporting_claims.claim: The rules that reach an EU shop, read from their official texts, are data requirements (a field, a history, a dated event, a structured document or a record) that belong in a named system of record, not page requirements.
Any rule can be read as a requirement by four questions (scope; data; system of record and channels; date and test), which turn it into a requirement card with an owner.

Rules are public years before they apply, their dates slip while scope holds, transposition multiplies them and partners enforce them first, so a merchant keeps one calendar with an owner per row who owns the fact, read against the official source each quarter.

The hosted platform absorbs some rules (the button, the banner, its checkout's card scope, its own pages' accessibility) but never the merchant's data rows, and how much compliance machinery a merchant needs grows with its size and role.

role.contribution: Turns the rules that reach a shop into data requirements with dates, places each in a system of record with a test and an owner on one calendar, and performs the part's closing (the published chapter does not yet do so: it ends with one sentence on Part VIII being complete and the hand-off to Part IX).

additional_patterns.applies_to: the rules, grouped by what they touch

flow.rationale: Four rules met late through four doors state the problem; the method comes next because every later section uses its four questions, and the rules section applies it to each instrument in turn. The calendar can only collect rules the reader has met, and one of its rows is taken through the whole method while the questions are fresh. The Long Fuse follows the calendar directly because it reads the calendar's rows for why they arrive late; the US contrast then marks the edge of the EU model before the choices. The choices answer the Long Fuse's last lesson (the data rows stay with the merchant); stages say which choice fits when; the failures come last because each is a row or an event that lost its owner. Putting the calendar before the rules would list dates for rules not yet read as data; putting the worked row at the end, as published, left the method many pages behind.

hook.content: A rule about displaying an earlier price can require price history that the merchant has never stored; engineering then needs a data source, a collection process and a page change, and learning of the rule just before it applies leaves little time, even though the deadline has been public for years.

bridge.from_reader_world: The previous chapter's one-month clock for answering a deletion request: one legal duty with a date that a merchant discovers late when it has no map.
bridge.to_topic: The other rules with dates touch prices, returns, product details, invoices and unsold goods, and each can be read as data with an owner, a test and a date.

thesis_statement.text: Most rules that reach a shop are data requirements, not page requirements: for each, ask which data it needs, who owns that data, how the behavior will be tested and when it must work, and keep the rules in one calendar with an owner per row; the hosted platform absorbs some of them, never the merchant's data rows.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout (in full) and paragraph p02 (the four questions)

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: Four Rules Through Four Doors
sections.controlling_idea: Four rules reached Kestrel & Pine through four doors it did not own, although each had been public for years, and Noor answers with a regulatory calendar that has an owner per row.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the case the chapter answers: four data requirements met late through partners, and the calendar that replaces those doors.

transition_in.carries_over: The roadmap, which starts from four rules through four doors.
transition_in.introduces: The four rules themselves.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In February 2027 Noor Visser finds that four regulations reached engineering through four unrelated channels: GPSR product-safety fields through marketplace listing rejections in December 2024, the European Accessibility Act through an agency audit in May 2025, Belgian e-invoicing through a customer refusing PDFs in December 2025, and the ESPR ban on destroying unsold apparel through an auditor's newsletter in June 2026.

evidence.what: 310 employees, three countries; GPSR from 13 December 2024, Amazon.de and Zalando listing fields, three weeks of spreadsheet work by Milan Petrov; EAA from 28 June 2025, audit in May 2025 with about 140 findings (illustrative); Belgian structured invoices from 1 January 2026, whether binding on a Dutch supplier not settled by the sources, Peppol connected in six weeks; ESPR from 19 July 2026 for large enterprises, 'unsold' includes withdrawal returns, about 39% of returned items not resold as new, found by Sanne de Wit in June 2026.
evidence.shows: Each rule is a data requirement (fields, accessible pages, a structured invoice, a disposition record) that arrived through a partner rather than a plan.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: None of the four was a secret, since the product-safety, accessibility and sustainable-product rules had been published years earlier, and two applied because of the company's size, so Noor adds a regulatory calendar to Waypoint, the company's improvement program, with a named owner for every applicable requirement.

evidence.what: Figure 1: four doors (error log, agency, customer, newsletter) and the calendar on the wall.
evidence.shows: Shows that none of the doors was the company's own and that the calendar is.

transition_in.introduces: What they had in common and Noor's response.

sections.heading: How to Read a Law as a Requirement
sections.controlling_idea: A law is read as a requirement by four questions (scope; data; system of record and channels; date and test), and applied to eight rules most rows land in a system the merchant did not have or did not own.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the method the rest of the chapter applies and shows on eight rules that most obligations are data in a system of record.

flow.rationale: The questions first, then the table that applies them, then what the table's third column shows; the reading of the column needs the table before it.

transition_in.carries_over: Four rules met late through partners, and the calendar Noor wants.
transition_in.introduces: The method that turns each rule into a row: four questions.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A legal text is written for courts, so the translation follows four questions: who is in scope by role, size and place; what the rule requires in data terms (a field, a history, a document or a clock); which system of record holds it and which channels show it; and when it applies and how compliance is tested.

The method table applies the four questions to eight rules (prior price, withdrawal, product safety, e-invoicing, packaging, unsold-goods destruction, accessibility and AI transparency) as a preview the next section explains in full, linking each to its data requirement, system of record, channels and test, after glossing OMS, PIM, WMS, ViDA, PPWR, WCAG and EN 16931.

evidence.what: Method table: rule, data requirement, system of record, channels that must show it, test, for eight rules.
evidence.shows: Shows the method producing a field, a system and a test for each rule.

transition_in.introduces: Their application to eight rules in one table.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Most rows land in a system Kestrel & Pine did not have or did not own in 2026 (the PIM, the OMS, the price history, a disposition record), so regulation is one more reason the Waypoint hubs exist.

evidence.what: Figure 2: reading a law as a requirement, scope first, then the field or clock, the owning system, the channels, a test and a dated row with a name.
evidence.shows: Summarizes the method as the requirement card later sections use.

transition_in.introduces: What it says about the company's systems.

sections.heading: The Rules, by What They Touch
sections.controlling_idea: Each rule that reaches an EU shop, read from its official text, asks for a field, a history, a dated event or a record that belongs in a named system of record.

advances_thesis.how: Demonstrates on every instrument the chapter names that the obligation is data with a date in a system of record.

flow.rationale: Rules grouped by what they touch, in the order an order meets them: the purchase and its undoing (consumer law), paying, invoicing, listing on platforms, the product's life after sale, accessibility of the whole path, then the duties set by role (cyber and AI) and by contract (data). Each group opens with a short paragraph saying what it touches, then the instruments, then what they mean in data terms.

transition_in.carries_over: The method table's eight rows, each in one line.
transition_in.introduces: Each rule in full from its official text, grouped by what it touches.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The method table named eight rules in a line each, and this section reads every rule from its official text, grouped by what it touches in the order an order meets them.

Consumer protections affect both the purchase decision and the ability to undo it, so the checkout must make the commitment clear while returns and payment systems need the dates and records used to handle withdrawal.

transition_in.carries_over: The grouping by what the rules touch.
transition_in.introduces: The first group: the purchase and its undoing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Consumer Rights Directive sets three clocks and one string (14 days to withdraw, extended to 12 months if the trader fails to inform; a refund within 14 days of the notice; the 'order with obligation to pay' button), and the clocks need delivery, notice and receipt recorded as events, so Eva's exchange request of 19 April 2027 started her clock that day.

evidence.what: Directive 2011/83/EU, applying from 13 June 2014: withdrawal within 14 days, refund within 14 days of the notice, the order-button wording.
evidence.shows: The obligations are clocks that start on recorded events.

evidence.what: Eva's exchange request of 19 April 2027 started the clock that day, not on 22 April when the jacket reached Duiven.
evidence.shows: The event that starts the clock is the notice.

transition_in.carries_over: Commitment and withdrawal need dates and records.
transition_in.introduces: The directive's clocks and the events that start them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Omnibus Directive's prior-price rule makes a 30-day price history per SKU per country a legal record, so the lawful 'was' price after a €179 autumn campaign is €179, not €199, and a merchant whose prices live in seven copies cannot produce it.

evidence.what: Directive (EU) 2019/2161, from 28 May 2022: 'the lowest price applied by the trader during a period of time not shorter than 30 days prior to the application of the price reduction'; ranking parameters, review provenance and personalized prices.
evidence.shows: The rule is stated as data: a minimum over a dated history.

transition_in.introduces: The second consumer rule: the prior price and reviews.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Payment rules affect how a checkout verifies the payer, so the design must take authentication steps without losing the cart or mistaking an interrupted payment for a completed order.

transition_in.carries_over: Consumer law at the purchase and its undoing.
transition_in.introduces: Rules on paying.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: PSD2 and its technical standards require strong customer authentication when a payer initiates an electronic payment, with exemptions for low-value and low-risk remote transactions, which means a challenge mid-payment and an exemption strategy for saved cards.

evidence.what: Directive (EU) 2015/2366 from 13 January 2018; Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 from 14 September 2019; exemptions up to €30 and for low-risk transactions.
evidence.shows: The obligation lands in the checkout's payment step.

transition_in.introduces: The strong-customer-authentication rule.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Since 9 October 2025 euro-area banks apply verification of payee, so the company name on a B2B invoice must match the bank account.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2024/886.
evidence.shows: A data match between invoice and bank account becomes a requirement.

transition_in.introduces: Verification of the payee.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation are pending as of November 2026, with fraud liability for providers already known, so their dates will follow adoption while their scope is known.

evidence.what: Provisional agreement 27 November 2025, member states' confirmation 22 April 2026, still open in the Council's state of play of 29 October 2026; European Parliament, 21 November 2025, on liability.
evidence.shows: A pending rule is a calendar row with known scope and no date.
evidence.source: Council of the EU; European Parliament

transition_in.introduces: The payment rules still pending.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Electronic invoicing determines which structured invoice a partner or authority can receive and when, and for a Dutch brand selling to businesses in three countries the mandates as of November 2026 are Belgium from 1 January 2026, Germany from 2025 to 2028, a planned Dutch mandate from 2030 and ViDA from 1 July 2030.

evidence.what: Belgium: structured e-invoices over Peppol between VAT-registered businesses since 1 January 2026, fines of €1,500 to €5,000 for lacking the means (FPS Finance); Germany: receiving since 1 January 2025, issuing from 1 January 2027 for German-established issuers above €800,000, all from 2028 (BMF FAQ); the Netherlands: domestic mandate planned from 1 July 2030 and reporting from 1 July 2031 (Rijksoverheid, 11 September 2026); ViDA: e-invoicing-based reporting for cross-border B2B supplies from 1 July 2030 (Council Directive (EU) 2025/516).
evidence.shows: The invoicing rules are a structured document with a date per country.
evidence.source: Restored from the chapter as published before commit db413120

transition_in.introduces: Invoicing: the mandates.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The mandates are domestic in scope: the German one does not bind a Dutch issuer, the sources do not settle whether the Belgian one reaches a Dutch supplier without a Belgian establishment, and business customers in both countries can demand the format.

evidence.what: Consistency items 5 and 17: the Belgian mandate's reach to a Dutch supplier is unsettled; the German mandate binds German-established issuers.
evidence.shows: Scope depends on establishment, while partners enforce the format regardless.

transition_in.carries_over: The four mandates and their dates.
transition_in.introduces: Who they bind, and why the format is needed anyway.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A marketplace needs to know who is selling and to make product information available to buyers, which creates seller and product records the merchant must keep consistent across channels.

transition_in.introduces: Platforms and marketplaces.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Digital Services Act requires a marketplace to obtain and verify each trader's identity, payment account, trade-register number and self-certification before it may sell, which for a merchant on three marketplaces is one onboarding data set kept current three times.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 from 17 February 2024, Art. 25, 30 and 31.
evidence.shows: The obligation is a data set per trader per marketplace.

transition_in.introduces: The DSA's trader-traceability rule.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The GPSR requires every distance offer to show the manufacturer's name and address, the responsible person's where the manufacturer is outside the EU, identification with a picture and warnings in the consumer's language, which in data terms is four mandatory attributes per product owned by the PIM, syndicated everywhere and blocking publication when missing.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2023/988 from 13 December 2024, Art. 19 and 22(9).
evidence.shows: The obligation is four attributes per product with one owning system.

transition_in.introduces: The product data set.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Product obligations continue after sale, so a merchant needs records of materials, packaging and the fate of unsold goods.

transition_in.introduces: The product's life after sale.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ESPR prohibits from 19 July 2026 the destruction of unsold apparel, accessories and footwear by large enterprises (medium from 2030, micro and small exempt) and requires operators that discard unsold products to disclose the number, weight, reasons and destination each year.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2024/1781, Art. 25(1) and Art. 24; Annex VII.
evidence.shows: The obligation is a disposition record and a yearly report.

transition_in.introduces: The destruction ban and disclosure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ESPR also defines the digital product passport with a registry of identifiers due by 19 July 2026, while which product groups come first awaits delegated acts and textiles around 2027 is an assumption.

transition_in.introduces: The passport, the regulation's second data requirement.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2024/1781, Art. 13: registry of identifiers by 19 July 2026; delegated acts not yet adopted.
evidence.shows: The passport is product data with a date still to be set.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For an apparel brand the disposition of every unsold or returned unit is a record with legal weight, and the PIM becomes the passport's source.

transition_in.introduces: What they mean in systems.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The PPWR makes producers responsible for packaging they first place on a member state's market from 12 August 2026, with fees computed from packaging weight by material per country of sale, so the product, the shipment and the order each carry part of the data.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2025/40, Art. 12 and 45; Germany's LUCID register (Dutch and Belgian schemes not verified).
evidence.shows: Packaging duty is data by material per country.

transition_in.introduces: Packaging data.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Customers must be able to use the whole purchasing path, including identification and payment, so an accessible product page is of little help when a vendor's checkout widget blocks the order.

transition_in.introduces: Accessibility of the whole path.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The European Accessibility Act covers e-commerce services from 28 June 2025, exempting microenterprises, and because it covers identification and payment, every embedded widget on the path to the order is in scope, so vendor conformance statements become a procurement item and the theme is audited per release.

evidence.what: Directive (EU) 2019/882: microenterprise exemption (fewer than 10 persons, at most €2 million), products in use until 28 June 2030, 'perceivable, operable, understandable and robust'; WCAG 2.1 AA in practice.
evidence.shows: The obligation reaches every vendor component on the path.

transition_in.introduces: The Accessibility Act's scope.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Security and AI rules assign duties by the service a business provides and the systems it uses, so the merchant first identifies its role.

sections.heading: The Long Fuse: Why Deadlines Arrive Late
sections.controlling_idea: Every row was public years before it applied, and five lessons follow: dates slip while scope holds, transposition multiplies the calendar, partners enforce first, courts and appeals are calendar events, and the platform absorbs some rules but never the data rows.

advances_thesis.how: Explains why a calendar with owners is needed and what the platform does not take off the merchant.

flow.rationale: The life of a row first, then the five lessons it supports, ending with the one that limits what the platform covers, which leads to the choices.

transition_in.carries_over: The calendar's rows, including the one taken through the method.
transition_in.introduces: The life each row had and why merchants meet them late.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every row had the same life (proposal, adopted text, often transposition, application, enforcement), usually two to four years from publication to application, and the evidence supports five lessons.

evidence.what: Figure 3: the Long Fuse, a rule public years before it applies, noticed by a calendar at adoption and by others at enforcement.
evidence.shows: Shows where a calendar notices a rule and where a merchant without one does.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Dates slip while scope holds, as the AI Act's high-risk dates, the PCI Council's script requirements and the Dutch e-invoicing mandate show, so a merchant plans the capability to the scope and schedules it to the date.

evidence.what: AI Act high-risk dates moved by more than a year (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744); PCI script requirements softened weeks before; Dutch mandate moved to 2030.
evidence.shows: Dates move, scope stays.

transition_in.introduces: The first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Transposition multiplies the calendar, because a directive becomes national laws with their own dates, so a merchant selling in three countries keeps three calendars.

transition_in.introduces: The second.

evidence.what: E-invoicing in Belgium (2026), Germany (2025-2028) and the Netherlands (planned 2030) under one EU framework; NIS2 in the Netherlands in August 2026.
evidence.shows: One directive, several national dates.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Partners enforce before regulators do, through marketplace listing fields, refused PDFs and label standards in purchasing conditions, so the Pulled Rug and the Long Fuse are often one event seen from two sides.

transition_in.introduces: The third.

evidence.what: Marketplaces turning the GPSR and DSA into listing fields; a business customer refusing PDFs; retail chains writing label standards into purchasing conditions.
evidence.shows: Partners set the effective date.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Courts and appeals are calendar events too, as Wayfair, the vacated click-to-cancel rule and the pending Data Privacy Framework appeal show, so a watch row is a real row.

transition_in.introduces: The fourth.

evidence.what: South Dakota v. Wayfair (21 June 2018); the Eighth Circuit vacating the FTC click-to-cancel rule (July 2025); appeal C-703/25 P against the Data Privacy Framework.
evidence.shows: Court decisions create or remove obligations on a date.
evidence.source: Cornell LII; Kelley Drye via JD Supra; Official Journal

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The platform absorbs some rules (the button, the cookie banner, the withdrawal flow, its checkout's card scope, its pages' accessibility) but not the merchant's price history, product-safety fields, packaging reports, disposition records or deletion fan-out, so the rows that remain are the data rows.

transition_in.introduces: The fifth, on what the platform takes off the merchant.

evidence.what: Figure 4: the platform carries the button, banner and card shield; the merchant carries price history, safety fields, packaging reports and disposition records.
evidence.shows: Shows why reacting leaves the data rows uncovered once they exist.

sections.heading: In Practice: The United States as the Contrast
sections.controlling_idea: The United States shows a different shape of law (state rules, statutes and lawsuits where the EU has regulations), so a platform serving both regions needs a tax engine, a consent record for both models and the same onboarding data twice.

advances_thesis.how: Marks the boundary of the EU model the calendar holds.

transition_in.carries_over: The EU calendar and the Long Fuse lessons, one of which drew on a US court decision.
transition_in.introduces: A region where the law has a different shape.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The calendar holds EU and national rules and the Long Fuse drew on one US decision, while a European merchant selling into the United States meets few federal rules, many state ones and lawsuits where the EU has regulations, starting with sales tax, which since Wayfair is a tax-engine problem.

evidence.what: South Dakota v. Wayfair, 21 June 2018; thresholds of $100,000 or 200 transactions; marketplace-facilitator laws.
evidence.shows: Tax obligations created by a court decision.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The INFORM Consumers Act requires marketplaces to collect, verify and disclose high-volume sellers' data, a mirror of DSA Art. 30.

evidence.what: Effective 27 June 2023; $20,000 disclosure threshold; $53,088 per violation.
evidence.shows: The same onboarding data under a US statute.

transition_in.introduces: Marketplace sellers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Reviews, accessibility and privacy follow other shapes: an FTC rule against fake reviews, accessibility exposure through litigation, and an opt-out privacy model across at least 19 state laws.

evidence.what: FTC rule of 14 August 2024; 5,114 suits in 2025, 70% against e-commerce (UsableNet, vendor figure); at least 19 state privacy laws (IAPP, 2025).
evidence.shows: US exposure comes from lawsuits and state laws.

transition_in.introduces: Reviews, accessibility and privacy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A platform serving both regions needs a tax engine, a consent record that expresses both models and the same onboarding data twice.

transition_in.introduces: What they require of a platform serving both regions.

flow.rationale: Four US differences (tax, sellers, reviews and accessibility and privacy), then what they require of a platform serving both regions.

sections.heading: The Choices: Four Ways to Run Compliance
sections.controlling_idea: A merchant can run compliance by reacting, by one owner with a calendar, by a calendar with requirement cards tied to the system-of-record map, or by a compliance function, and the third, built from the second, fits once it owns a PIM, an OMS or a price history.

advances_thesis.how: Sets the calendar the thesis recommends against its alternatives and says when each fits.

flow.rationale: The four approaches from lightest to heaviest, then the table and the recommendation that needs all four.

transition_in.carries_over: The data rows that stay with the merchant (the Long Fuse's last lesson), after the US contrast.
transition_in.introduces: The four ways a merchant can organize to keep them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The data rows stay with the merchant, which has four ways to keep them, and the first, reacting when someone complains with no calendar at all, is the default and nearly adequate for a Starting-stage shop on a hosted platform in one country.

evidence.what: Reacting when someone complains: no calendar, rules arriving through partners and fines.
evidence.shows: The lightest approach and when it is nearly adequate.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: One owner with one calendar reviewed quarterly is cheap and removes the surprise but does not put the fields in the systems.

transition_in.introduces: The first approach with a calendar.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A calendar plus requirement cards tied to the entity-owner table, with tests in the release process, is where an Omnichannel merchant should be, because that is when rules land in systems it owns.

transition_in.introduces: A calendar with cards and tests.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A compliance function with counsel and tooling is right for a group or a vendor and, at Kestrel & Pine's size, the Giant's Boots.

evidence.what: Cost (illustrative), what each approach catches and misses, and when it is right.
evidence.shows: Puts the four approaches on the same criteria.

transition_in.introduces: The heaviest approach.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author recommends the third approach, built from the second, the quarter the merchant first owns a PIM, an OMS or a price history, because the calendar is a management artifact and the cards are what engineering can test.

transition_in.introduces: The author's choice and when to make it.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: Scope follows size and role, so each scale stage needs a different approach, and growth is a change of scope that a calendar row should name.

advances_thesis.how: Ties the choice of approach and the rows that switch on to the merchant's size and role.

transition_in.carries_over: The recommendation tied to owning a PIM, OMS or price history.
transition_in.introduces: How the right approach changes across the four scale stages.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Scope follows size: a microenterprise is exempt from the Accessibility Act, a small enterprise from the ESPR ban, a Dutch company below the small-business threshold from the planned e-invoicing mandate, and a retailer that becomes a marketplace operator picks up DSA and NIS2 duties that day, so a row should say which size or role triggers it.

evidence.what: Stage, typical approach, what becomes necessary, warning signs, for Starting, Growing, Omnichannel and Group, with Kestrel & Pine's dated arrivals as warning signs.
evidence.shows: Shows the approach growing with stage and the triggers that move a merchant up.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Three failures recur (a deadline discovered late, a clock nobody started, a partner's deadline before the law's), each with a detection and a recovery that end in an owned row or event.

advances_thesis.how: Shows what happens when a row has no owner or an event no real date, and how to recover.

flow.rationale: Three failures with the same shape (detection, recovery), from the calendar level to the event level to the partner.

transition_in.carries_over: The approach and the rows that switch on with size and role.
transition_in.introduces: Rows and events that fail, and how to recover.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A deadline discovered late is recovered capability first and evidence second, because Belgium's tolerance spared only businesses that could show timely steps, and then the merchant asks which other rows have no owner.

evidence.what: FPS Finance tolerance of December 2025: 'under no circumstances' a general postponement.
evidence.shows: Evidence of timely steps is part of recovery.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A clock nobody started, such as a withdrawal notice typed in four days late, is detected by a refund-age report on the notice date and recovered by every notice channel creating the event with its real date.

transition_in.introduces: A late event.

evidence.what: A withdrawal notice received by e-mail and typed into the returns portal four days later.
evidence.shows: The clock runs from the real notice, not the entry.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A partner's deadline before the law's is detected by an owner reading partner notices and recovered by making the partner's date the row's date, because the partner is the enforcer that matters.

transition_in.introduces: An early partner date.

evidence.what: A marketplace requiring a field months before a regulation applies; a chain demanding a label standard the law never mentions.
evidence.shows: The partner's date is the effective date.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The opening's price rule is the chapter's pattern: a public rule became an emergency because its data had no owner, and the same is true of the withdrawal clocks, the product-safety fields, the structured invoice and the disposition record; read as requirements and kept on one calendar, they are ordinary engineering with a date. For the part: the Card-Testing Night, the Request From Ghent and four rules through four doors look like three disciplines with a product each, but in each something from outside used or demanded what the merchant already had, the platform did what its vendor promised, and the gap was an item nobody had on a list with an owner.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant that reads rules this way keeps one calendar with owners who own the facts and puts the field, history or clock into its owning system before the date; for the part, Kestrel & Pine answered with three lists on Noor Visser's ownership map (the April 2027 security baseline, the privacy map with the October 2027 request orchestrator, the March 2027 regulatory calendar), and a reader can extend their own map with the same three columns.

callback.to: The introduction's price rule that needs a price history the shop never stored; and, for the part, the part opening's checkout that accepts a real purchase and 48,000 attempts with stolen cards by the same behavior.
callback.how: Paragraph p60 answers the chapter's opening price rule; p65, under the heading Closing Part VIII, returns to the part opening's checkout and names each chapter's case; p66 and p67 perform the part closing's so-what and take-away.

takeaway.content: Add three columns to your ownership map: for every identity and key, its owner and scope; for every system that holds personal data, its legal role, the action a request requires and its retention clock; for every rule that applies, its data, system of record, test, date and owner. Start with the integrations that have no named owner, because each is a key, a data flow and a fact at once.
